claim: PNG protein is present in stage 10 oocytes arrested in prophase I.
source: PNG and PLU were observed in extracts from stage 10 oocytes, which are arrested in prophase I (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1A demonstrating PNG protein detection in stage 10 oocytes.

claim: PLU protein is present in stage 10 oocytes arrested in prophase I.
source: PNG and PLU were observed in extracts from stage 10 oocytes, which are arrested in prophase I (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1A demonstrating PLU protein detection in stage 10 oocytes.

claim: GNU protein is undetectable in stage 10 oocytes.
source: In contrast, GNU was undetectable in stage 10, but was present as maturation occurred in stage 13 (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1B showing absence of GNU protein in stage 10 oocytes.

claim: GNU protein is present in stage 13 oocytes.
source: In contrast, GNU was undetectable in stage 10, but was present as maturation occurred in stage 13 (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1B demonstrating GNU protein detection in stage 13 oocytes.

claim: PNG, PLU, and GNU protein levels are high in mature stage 14 oocytes arrested at metaphase I.
source: The protein levels of all three subunits were high in mature oocytes (stage 14), which are arrested at metaphase I (Figure 1A,B), a conclusion supported by quantitative mass spectrometry experiments (Kronja et al., 2014a).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figures 1A and 1B and cited mass spectrometry data from Kronja et al., 2014a.

claim: GNU protein accumulation during oocyte maturation requires CDK1 activity.
source: The accumulation of PNG complex components during oocyte maturation could require CDK1 activity, because in twine mutant stage 14 oocytes, PNG complex proteins did not accumulate (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 showing reduced PNG complex protein levels in twine mutant oocytes, which lack Cdc25 phosphatase required for CycB/CDK1 activation.

claim: twine encodes a homolog of the Cdc25 phosphatase required to activate CycB/CDK1 during oogenesis.
source: twine encodes a homolog of the Cdc25 phosphatase required to activate CycB/CDK1 during oogenesis (Courtot et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citation to Courtot et al., 1992.

claim: GNU protein exhibits a mobility shift from slower to faster forms between 20 and 30 minutes after egg activation.
source: Notably, a change in GNU mobility occurred during egg activation. A slower mobility form of GNU present following oocyte maturation was replaced by a faster mobility form between 20 and 30 min after hypotonic buffer treatment.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 1B showing GNU mobility changes during in vitro egg activation time course.

claim: The slower mobility forms of GNU are due to phosphorylation.
source: These changes are consistent with a loss of phosphorylation, and indeed the slower mobility forms of GNU were previously noted in oocytes and shown to be due to phosphorylation (Renault et al., 2003; Zhang et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Renault et al., 2003; Zhang et al., 2004) and by phosphatase sensitivity data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The upper bands of GNU disappear when okadaic acid is omitted from the native lysis buffer.
source: The upper bands of GNU disappeared when okadaic acid (OA), a PP2A phosphatase inhibitor, was omitted from the native lysis buffer, implying that the slower mobility is due to phosphorylation and sensitive to phosphatase (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 showing GNU mobility changes with and without okadaic acid.

claim: CycB protein levels decrease 20 minutes after egg activation.
source: CycB was accumulated and its levels decreased 20 min after egg activation, beginning to increase again at 40 min.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 1B showing CycB protein levels at different time points after egg activation.

claim: CycB protein levels correlate with oscillation of H1 kinase activity.
source: The levels of CycB correlate with oscillation of H1 kinase activity.
evidence: Supported by H1 kinase activity assay and CycB immunoblot data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: At 20 minutes post activation, the majority of eggs are completing meiosis.
source: The 20 min post activation time point marks the point when the majority of eggs were completing meiosis, and by 30 min nearly 60% had completed meiosis.
evidence: Supported by quantification of meiotic stages in activated eggs shown in Figure 1C.

claim: GNU transitions from fully phosphorylated to hypophosphorylated form between early and late anaphase of meiosis II.
source: The transition from the fully phosphorylated to the hypophosphorylated form was observed to occur between early and late anaphase of meiosis II (anaphase II).
evidence: Supported by single oocyte analysis data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 correlating GNU mobility with meiotic stage.

claim: GNU becomes dephosphorylated when CycB levels decline, H1 kinase activity decreases, and meiosis is completed.
source: Thus we conclude GNU becomes dephosphorylated when CycB levels decline, H1 kinase activity decreases, and meiosis is completed.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from correlation of GNU dephosphorylation timing with CycB decline, H1 kinase activity decrease, and meiosis completion shown in Figures 1B and 1C.

claim: SMG protein accumulation requires PNG activity.
source: Because smg maternal mRNA translational activation is a downstream target dependent on PNG, appearance of SMG protein after egg activation requires PNG activity (Tadros et al., 2007; Kronja et al., 2014b; Eichhorn et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Tadros et al., 2007; Kronja et al., 2014b; Eichhorn et al., 2016) demonstrating PNG-dependent SMG translation.

claim: SMG protein starts to accumulate 20 to 30 minutes after hypotonic buffer treatment.
source: Strikingly, we found that SMG started to accumulate 20 to 30 min after hypotonic buffer treatment, when GNU is dephosphorylated and meiosis completed (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figures 1A and 1B showing SMG protein appearance at 20-30 minutes post-activation.

claim: Nine predicted CycB/CDK1 sites (S/T-P) exist in GNU.
source: There are nine predicted CycB/CDK1 sites (S/T-P) in GNU, and peptides containing these residues were the phosphopeptides most frequently recovered (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: All nine CDK1 sites in GNU were detected as phosphorylated in stage 14 oocytes.
source: All nine sites were detected as phosphorylated, with significant Ascore values (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1 with Ascore values indicating phosphorylation.

claim: Eight of the nine CycB/CDK1 sites in GNU are in a region predicted to be disordered.
source: Eight of the nine CycB/CDK1 sites are in a region in the GNU protein predicted to be disordered by four different algorithms (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by disorder prediction analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 using four different algorithms.

claim: Purified active CycB/CDK1 directly phosphorylates recombinant GNU in vitro.
source: We found that purified active CycB/CDK1 directly phosphorylated recombinant GNU (Figure 2B), resulting in its mobility shift-up on SDS-PAGE.
evidence: Supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 2B demonstrating radioactive phosphate incorporation into GNU by CycB/CDK1.

claim: Alanine substitution of all nine CDK1 sites in GNU (GNU-9A) blocks phosphorylation and mobility shift by CycB/CDK1.
source: When we introduced mutations that substituted alanine into all nine CDK1 sites of GNU (GNU-9A), GNU phosphorylation and mobility shift-up by CycB/CDK1 were blocked (Figure 2B), indicating that GNU indeed is a direct substrate of CycB/CDK1 in vitro.
evidence: Supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 2B comparing wild-type GNU and GNU-9A phosphorylation by CycB/CDK1.

claim: GNU phosphorylated by CycB/CDK1 does not elevate PNG kinase activity.
source: Strikingly, GNU that was phosphorylated by CycB/CDK1 prior to addition to the kinase assay did not elevate PNG kinase activity (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by in vitro PNG kinase activity assay data shown in Figure 2C comparing unphosphorylated and CycB/CDK1-phosphorylated GNU.

claim: CycB/CDK1 phosphorylation of GNU blocks the ability of GNU to activate PNG kinase.
source: This showed that CycB/CDK1-phosphorylation of GNU blocks the ability of GNU to activate PNG kinase.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from in vitro PNG kinase activity assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: PNG, PLU and GNU co-immunoprecipitate in Sf9 cells, indicating their physical association as a complex.
source: As previously shown, PNG, PLU and GNU co-immunoprecipitate, indicating their physical association as a complex in Sf9 cells (Figure 2D) (Lee et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2D and citation to Lee et al., 2003.

claim: When Sf9 cells expressing the PNG kinase complex are treated with okadaic acid, GNU is hyper-phosphorylated and dissociates from the PNG-PLU sub-complex.
source: In contrast, when the cells expressing the PNG kinase complex were treated with OA, which causes an M-phase-like state (Yamashita et al., 1990), GNU was hyper-phosphorylated and dissociated from the PNG-PLU sub-complex (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2D comparing okadaic acid-treated and untreated cells, and citation to Yamashita et al., 1990.

claim: Alanine mutations in the CDK1 consensus sequences suppress hyperphosphorylation of GNU and restore interaction of GNU with the PNG-PLU sub-complex in okadaic acid-treated cells.
source: Remarkably, introducing alanine mutations into the CDK1 consensus sequences suppressed the hyperphosphorylation of GNU and restored interaction of GNU with the PNG-PLU sub-complex in the OA-treated cells (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 4 comparing GNU-WT and GNU-9A in okadaic acid-treated cells.

claim: Phosphorylation of GNU on CDK1 target sites prevents its interaction with the PNG-PLU sub-complex.
source: These results indicate that phosphorylation of GNU on CDK1 target sites prevents its interaction with the PNG-PLU sub-complex.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: CDK1 inhibits PNG kinase activity via preventing assembly of the full PNG kinase complex.
source: Together with the results of the in vitro kinase assays (Figure 2C), this leads to the conclusion that CDK1 inhibits PNG kinase activity via preventing assembly of the full PNG kinase complex, which is essential for its kinase activation (Lee et al., 2003).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from in vitro kinase assay data (Figure 2C) and immunoprecipitation data (Figure 2D), with citation to Lee et al., 2003.

claim: GNU-GFP WT fusion protein complements the gnu mutant to produce embryos in which normal embryonic mitoses occur.
source: The GNU-GFP WT fusion protein complemented the gnu mutant to produce embryos in which normal embryonic mitoses occurred (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by embryo phenotype analysis shown in Figure 3A and quantification in Figure 3B.

claim: GNU-GFP 9A has partial function in rescuing gnu mutant embryos.
source: GNU-GFP 9A had partial function: all embryos underwent mitosis, but some exhibited the phenotype of weak alleles of png complex subunits, whereas others were able to complete the syncytial mitotic divisions (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by embryo phenotype analysis and quantification shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: Levels of CycB protein in stage 14 oocytes are significantly higher when GNU-GFP 9A is expressed compared to GNU-GFP WT.
source: We found that levels of CycB protein in stage 14 oocytes were significantly higher when GNU-GFP 9A was expressed compared to GNU-GFP WT (Figure 4A,B, five replicates, p=0.03 for line 2–7 and p=0.01 for line 2–8, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data and quantification shown in Figure 4A and 4B with statistical analysis from five biological replicates.

claim: GNU-GFP 9A migrates faster than GNU-GFP WT in stage 14 oocytes.
source: As expected, in stage 14 oocytes, GNU-GFP 9A migrated faster than GNU-GFP WT, indicating that indeed the 9A mutant was not phosphorylated at CycB/CDK1 sites stage 14 oocytes (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5 comparing GNU-GFP WT and 9A mobility.

claim: GNU-GFP 9A, but not GNU-GFP WT, is detected in PNG immunoprecipitates from stage 14 oocytes.
source: Strikingly, GNU-GFP 9A, but not GNU-GFP WT, was detected at low levels but consistently in PNG immunoprecipitates from stage 14 oocytes (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5 comparing GNU-GFP WT and 9A binding to PNG in stage 14 oocytes.

claim: Interaction between the PNG-PLU sub-complex and GNU is prevented by phosphorylation of CDK1 target sites on GNU.
source: Taken together, these results confirm that interaction between the PNG-PLU sub-complex and GNU is prevented by phosphorylation of CDK1 target sites on GNU.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5 and other supporting data.

claim: The phosphorylation-resistant form of GNU results in premature elevation of Cyclin B protein levels, consistent with PNG kinase being prematurely active.
source: The phosphorylation-resistant form of GNU is able to associate with PNG and results in premature elevation of Cyc B protein levels, consistent with PNG kinase being prematurely active.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from CycB protein level data (Figure 4A,B) and PNG-GNU interaction data (Figure 5).

claim: In GNU-GFP 9A oocytes, the condensed phase of metaphase I persists longer than in wild type.
source: In the GNU-GFP 9A oocytes the condensed phase of metaphase I persisted longer than in wild type, and the metaphase I/anaphase I transition was delayed (Figure 4C, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by meiotic progression analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The metaphase I/anaphase I transition is delayed in GNU-GFP 9A oocytes.
source: In the GNU-GFP 9A oocytes the condensed phase of metaphase I persisted longer than in wild type, and the metaphase I/anaphase I transition was delayed (Figure 4C, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by meiotic progression analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The GNU-GFP 9A form results in defects in meiotic chromosome segregation.
source: In addition to delays in progression through meiosis, the GNU-GFP 9A form resulted in defects in meiotic chromosome segregation.
evidence: Supported by chromosome morphology analysis shown in Figure 4D and quantification in Figure 4E.

claim: In GNU-GFP 9A oocytes, chromosomes are aberrant at metaphase I in 19-23% of oocytes.
source: The morphology of chromosomes after egg activation at metaphase I was aberrant in 19–23% of the oocytes.
evidence: Supported by quantification of chromosome morphology defects shown in Figure 4E.

claim: In GNU-GFP 9A oocytes, unequal segregation of chromosomes occurs in up to 23% of oocytes.
source: Later, as meiosis was completed, the size and DAPI-staining intensity was uneven in up to 23% of oocytes, reflecting unequal segregation of chromosomes during the meiotic divisions (Figure 4D,E, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by chromosome segregation analysis shown in Figure 4D and quantification in Figure 4E.

claim: Proper levels of CycB protein are necessary for the accuracy of meiotic divisions in the oocyte.
source: Thus we conclude that proper levels of CycB protein and possibly other PNG targets are necessary for the accuracy of meiotic divisions in the oocyte.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from meiotic defects observed in GNU-GFP 9A oocytes with elevated CycB levels (Figures 4C, 4D, 4E).

claim: GNU protein levels decrease in fertilized embryos (0-2 hr) compared to stage 14 oocytes in control (png1058/+) genotype.
source: In contrast to control embryos (png1058/+) in which GNU protein levels were largely decreased, its levels remained high in png mutant fertilized embryos (png1058/ png1058), despite its becoming dephosphorylated (Figure 6).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 6B comparing GNU levels in stage 14 oocytes and embryos.

claim: GNU protein levels remain high in png mutant fertilized embryos (png1058/png1058).
source: In contrast to control embryos (png1058/+) in which GNU protein levels were largely decreased, its levels remained high in png mutant fertilized embryos (png1058/ png1058), despite its becoming dephosphorylated (Figure 6).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 6B comparing GNU levels in control and png mutant embryos.

claim: The decrease of GNU protein requires PNG kinase activity.
source: Here we found that the decrease of GNU protein requires PNG kinase activity.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from immunoblot data shown in Figure 6B comparing GNU levels in control and png mutant embryos.

claim: GNU becomes dephosphorylated after egg activation in both control and png mutant embryos.
source: In contrast to control embryos (png1058/+) in which GNU protein levels were largely decreased, its levels remained high in png mutant fertilized embryos (png1058/ png1058), despite its becoming dephosphorylated (Figure 6).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 6B showing GNU mobility shift in both control and png mutant embryos.

claim: Control of PNG kinase activity via GNU phosphorylation by CycB/CDK1 links meiotic completion and translational control of maternal mRNA.
source: Thus we propose that control of PNG kinase activity via GNU phosphorylation by CycB/CDK1 links meiotic completion and translational control of maternal mRNA to coordinate their timing precisely during egg activation (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a synthesis and interpretation of all the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Active PNG leads to decreased GNU protein levels.
source: Active PNG leads to decreased GNU protein levels.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 6 showing GNU stabilization in png mutants.

claim: PNG kinase activity is constrained to the short developmental window of the oocyte-to-embryo transition.
source: This makes a negative feedback to shut down PNG kinase activity, thereby ensuring PNG kinase activity is constrained to the short developmental window of the oocyte-to-embryo transition (Figure 7).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from GNU destabilization data (Figure 6) and the overall regulatory mechanism.

claim: GNU protein accumulation during oocyte maturation relies on translational activation of its mRNA.
source: Our previous genome-wide study showed that GNU protein accumulation during oocytes maturation relies on translational activation of its mRNA (Kronja et al., 2014a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kronja et al., 2014a.

claim: GNU translational activation during oocyte maturation is dependent on CDK1 activity.
source: Although the regulatory mechanisms for gnu translational activation remain to be defined, it is clearly dependent on CDK1, but not MOS, activity.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 showing reduced GNU in twine mutants and Figure 2—figure supplement 3 showing normal GNU in mos mutants.

claim: GNU translational activation during oocyte maturation is not dependent on MOS activity.
source: Although the regulatory mechanisms for gnu translational activation remain to be defined, it is clearly dependent on CDK1, but not MOS, activity.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3 showing normal GNU levels in mos mutants.

claim: Ectopic GNU protein expression in stage 11 oocytes causes png-dependent premature CycB protein expression.
source: Ectopic GNU protein expression in early stage oocytes, which are in prophase I, causes png-dependent premature CycB protein expression and actin disorganization (Renault et al., 2003; Vardy and Orr-Weaver, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Renault et al., 2003 and Vardy and Orr-Weaver, 2007.

claim: Ectopic GNU protein expression in stage 11 oocytes causes png-dependent actin disorganization.
source: Ectopic GNU protein expression in early stage oocytes, which are in prophase I, causes png-dependent premature CycB protein expression and actin disorganization (Renault et al., 2003; Vardy and Orr-Weaver, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Renault et al., 2003 and Vardy and Orr-Weaver, 2007.

claim: GNU remains hyperphosphorylated in eggs laid from sra mutant mothers.
source: Analysis of the phosphorylation state of GNU in mutants for the calcipressin Sarah (sra) or the meiosis-specific APC/C activator Cortex (cort) showed that GNU remains hyperphosphorylated in eggs laid from both types of mutant mothers (Krauchunas et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Krauchunas et al., 2013.

claim: GNU remains hyperphosphorylated in eggs laid from cort mutant mothers.
source: Analysis of the phosphorylation state of GNU in mutants for the calcipressin Sarah (sra) or the meiosis-specific APC/C activator Cortex (cort) showed that GNU remains hyperphosphorylated in eggs laid from both types of mutant mothers (Krauchunas et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Krauchunas et al., 2013.

claim: sra mutant eggs are arrested in anaphase I.
source: Interestingly, both of these mutants fail to complete meiosis, with sra mutant eggs arrested in anaphase I, and cort mutants arrested in metaphase II (Page and Orr-Weaver, 1996; Horner et al., 2006; Takeo et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Page and Orr-Weaver, 1996; Horner et al., 2006; Takeo et al., 2006.

claim: cort mutant eggs are arrested in metaphase II.
source: Interestingly, both of these mutants fail to complete meiosis, with sra mutant eggs arrested in anaphase I, and cort mutants arrested in metaphase II (Page and Orr-Weaver, 1996; Horner et al., 2006; Takeo et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Page and Orr-Weaver, 1996; Horner et al., 2006; Takeo et al., 2006.

claim: PNG and PLU protein levels are gradually decreased 2-4 hours after embryo laying.
source: Although PNG and PLU levels in embryos are gradually decreased 2–4 hr after laying (Elfring et al., 1997; Fenger et al., 2000) GNU seems to disappear after the completion of meiosis but before the initiation of embryogenesis.
evidence: Supported by citations to Elfring et al., 1997 and Fenger et al., 2000.

claim: GNU protein levels are decreased in unfertilized in vivo activated eggs.
source: This is evidenced by GNU protein levels being decreased in unfertilized in vivo activated eggs, which complete meiosis II but do not enter into the embryonic cycles.
evidence: This is stated as evidence for rapid GNU disappearance after meiosis completion, based on previous observations cited in Kronja et al., 2014b.

claim: GNU levels fail to decline in cort mutants.
source: We noted that GNU levels fail to decline in cort mutants (Kronja et al., 2014a), which lack one form of the APC/C.
evidence: Supported by citation to Kronja et al., 2014a.

claim: PP1 is capable of dephosphorylating GNU in mature oocytes.
source: Although it has been shown that PP1 is capable of dephosphorylating GNU in mature oocytes (Renault et al., 2003), PP2A also is a possible GNU phosphatase during the process, particularly given it is the major phosphatase that removes phosphates on CDK1 substrates in mitotic exit (Mochida et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Renault et al., 2003.

claim: PP2A is the major phosphatase that removes phosphates on CDK1 substrates in mitotic exit.
source: Although it has been shown that PP1 is capable of dephosphorylating GNU in mature oocytes (Renault et al., 2003), PP2A also is a possible GNU phosphatase during the process, particularly given it is the major phosphatase that removes phosphates on CDK1 substrates in mitotic exit (Mochida et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mochida et al., 2009.

claim: GNU 9A mutant protein binds to the PNG-PLU sub-complex even in high CDK activity.
source: This mutant protein binds to the PNG-PLU sub-complex even in high CDK activity, however, it does not activate PNG kinase to the full extent that wild-type GNU does.
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data in Figure 2D and kinase activity data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: GNU 9A mutant protein does not activate PNG kinase to the full extent that wild-type GNU does.
source: This mutant protein binds to the PNG-PLU sub-complex even in high CDK activity, however, it does not activate PNG kinase to the full extent that wild-type GNU does.
evidence: Supported by kinase activity data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and partial rescue data in Figure 3.

claim: A point mutation in the GNU N-terminal region (changing Pro 17 to Leu) retains ability to bind the PNG-PLU sub-complex but does not activate PNG kinase activity in vitro.
source: A point mutation in the GNU N-terminal region (changing Pro 17 to Leu) retains ability to bind the PNG-PLU sub-complex but not does not activate PNG kinase activity in vitro (Hara and Orr-Weaver, unpublished and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by unpublished data and kinase activity data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: PNG kinase regulates translation of hundreds of maternal mRNAs.
source: The PNG kinase is significant for the understanding of how a kinase can rapidly control translation of hundreds of mRNAs.
evidence: Supported by previous genome-wide studies cited in the manuscript (Kronja et al., 2014b; Eichhorn et al., 2016).

claim: CDK1 regulates both protein expression of PNG kinase complex components and PNG kinase activity.
source: Strikingly, a cell cycle regulator, CDK1, controls both.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from data showing CDK1-dependent GNU accumulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and CDK1-mediated inhibition of PNG activity (Figures 2B, 2C, 2D).

claim: CDK1 precisely regulates PNG kinase activity, coordinating cell cycle progression and translational landscape change during the oocyte-to-embryo transition.
source: This implies that CDK1 precisely regulates PNG kinase activity, a translational regulator, thus coordinating cell cycle progression and the translational landscape change during the oocyte-to-embryo transition.
evidence: This is a synthesis and interpretation of all the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In C. elegans, MBK-2 kinase is crucial for the oocyte-to-embryo transition.
source: In C. elegans another kinase, the MBK-2 member of the conserved DYRK family of dual specificity tyrosine kinases, like PNG is crucial for the oocyte-to-embryo transition.
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans development.

claim: MBK-2 activation is linked to the meiotic cell cycle by being downstream of the APC/C.
source: MBK-2 activation is linked to the meiotic cell cycle by being downstream of the APC/C (Parry and Singson, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Parry and Singson, 2011.

claim: MBK-2 controls proteolysis of oocyte proteins through the SCF E3 ubiquitin ligase.
source: MBK-2 controls proteolysis of oocyte proteins through the SCF E3 ubiquitin ligase (Robertson and Lin, 2013), and it also affects RNA granule dynamics and thus likely impacts translation (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Robertson and Lin, 2013.

claim: MBK-2 affects RNA granule dynamics and thus likely impacts translation.
source: MBK-2 controls proteolysis of oocyte proteins through the SCF E3 ubiquitin ligase (Robertson and Lin, 2013), and it also affects RNA granule dynamics and thus likely impacts translation (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2014.

claim: The oocyte-to-embryo transition involves extensive changes in mRNA translation.
source: The oocyte-to-embryo transition involves extensive changes in mRNA translation, regulated in Drosophila by the PNG kinase complex whose activity we show here to be under precise developmental control.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the oocyte-to-embryo transition and is supported by the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: PNG, PLU, and GNU are present in the mature oocyte.
source: Despite presence of the catalytic PNG subunit and the PLU and GNU activating subunits in the mature oocyte, GNU is phosphorylated at Cyclin B/CDK1sites and unable to bind PNG and PLU.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figures 1A and 1B.

claim: In mature oocytes, GNU is phosphorylated at Cyclin B/CDK1 sites and unable to bind PNG and PLU.
source: Despite presence of the catalytic PNG subunit and the PLU and GNU activating subunits in the mature oocyte, GNU is phosphorylated at Cyclin B/CDK1sites and unable to bind PNG and PLU.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data (Figure 2A), in vitro phosphorylation data (Figure 2B), and immunoprecipitation data (Figure 5).

claim: In vitro phosphorylation of GNU by CyclinB/CDK1 blocks activation of PNG.
source: In vitro phosphorylation of GNU by CyclinB/CDK1 blocks activation of PNG.
evidence: Supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Meiotic completion promotes GNU dephosphorylation and PNG kinase activation to regulate translation.
source: Meiotic completion promotes GNU dephosphorylation and PNG kinase activation to regulate translation.
evidence: Supported by correlation of GNU dephosphorylation with meiosis completion (Figures 1B, 1C) and SMG accumulation as indicator of PNG activation (Figure 1A, 1B).

claim: Replacement of GNU in the oocyte with a phosphorylation-resistant form promotes PNG-GNU complex formation.
source: The critical regulatory effect of phosphorylation is shown by replacement in the oocyte with a phosphorylation-resistant form of GNU, which promotes PNG-GNU complex formation, elevation of Cyclin B, and meiotic defects consistent with premature PNG activation.
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data (Figure 5), CycB level data (Figure 4A, 4B), and meiotic defect data (Figure 4C, 4D, 4E).

claim: Replacement of GNU in the oocyte with a phosphorylation-resistant form causes elevation of Cyclin B.
source: The critical regulatory effect of phosphorylation is shown by replacement in the oocyte with a phosphorylation-resistant form of GNU, which promotes PNG-GNU complex formation, elevation of Cyclin B, and meiotic defects consistent with premature PNG activation.
evidence: Supported by CycB level data shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: Replacement of GNU in the oocyte with a phosphorylation-resistant form causes meiotic defects consistent with premature PNG activation.
source: The critical regulatory effect of phosphorylation is shown by replacement in the oocyte with a phosphorylation-resistant form of GNU, which promotes PNG-GNU complex formation, elevation of Cyclin B, and meiotic defects consistent with premature PNG activation.
evidence: Supported by meiotic defect data shown in Figure 4C, 4D, and 4E.

claim: After PNG activation, GNU is destabilized, thus inactivating PNG.
source: After PNG activation GNU is destabilized, thus inactivating PNG.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 6 showing PNG-dependent GNU destabilization.

claim: The short-lived burst in PNG kinase activity links development with maternal mRNA translation and ensures irreversibility of the oocyte-to-embryo transition.
source: This short-lived burst in kinase activity links development with maternal mRNA translation and ensures irreversibility of the oocyte-to-embryo transition.
evidence: This is a synthesis and interpretation of all the experimental data showing temporal control of PNG activity.

claim: The onset of embryogenesis at the oocyte-to-embryo transition occurs in the absence of transcription.
source: The onset of embryogenesis at the oocyte-to-embryo transition occurs in the absence of transcription and thus requires remodeling of mRNA translation that alters the proteome (Tadros and Lipshitz, 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Tadros and Lipshitz, 2009.

claim: The oocyte-to-embryo transition requires remodeling of mRNA translation that alters the proteome.
source: The onset of embryogenesis at the oocyte-to-embryo transition occurs in the absence of transcription and thus requires remodeling of mRNA translation that alters the proteome (Tadros and Lipshitz, 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Tadros and Lipshitz, 2009.

claim: The immature oocyte is arrested at prophase of meiosis I in nearly all animals.
source: The immature oocyte is arrested at prophase of meiosis I (prophase I) in nearly all animals to permit oocyte differentiation, and this arrest is released as oocyte maturation initiates.
evidence: This is established knowledge about oocyte development across animal species.

claim: Oocytes arrest at metaphase of meiosis II in vertebrates.
source: Maturation leads to the oocyte entering the meiotic divisions and arresting at a second point, metaphase of meiosis II (metaphase II) in vertebrates and metaphase of meiosis I (metaphase I) in insects.
evidence: This is established knowledge about vertebrate oocyte development.

claim: Oocytes arrest at metaphase of meiosis I in insects.
source: Maturation leads to the oocyte entering the meiotic divisions and arresting at a second point, metaphase of meiosis II (metaphase II) in vertebrates and metaphase of meiosis I (metaphase I) in insects.
evidence: This is established knowledge about insect oocyte development.

claim: In Drosophila, egg activation can be independent of fertilization.
source: In many organisms egg activation is linked to fertilization, although it can be independent in organisms such as Drosophila (Horner and Wolfner, 2008b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Horner and Wolfner, 2008b.

claim: In most animal species, oocytes and early embryos are dependent on posttranscriptional control.
source: In contrast to somatic cells, in which transcription is a major source of gene expression changes, in most animal species oocytes and early embryos are dependent on posttranscriptional control (Walker et al., 1996; Potireddy et al., 2006; Chen et al., 2011; Krauchunas and Wolfner, 2013; Robertson and Lin, 2013; Kronja et al., 2014a, 2014b).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: In Drosophila, oocytes in early stages (from stage 5 to 12) are arrested at prophase I.
source: Oocytes in early stages (from stage 5 to 12) are arrested at prophase I.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila oocyte development.

claim: In Drosophila, oocytes in stage 13 undergo nuclear envelope breakdown.
source: Oocytes in stage 13 undergo nuclear envelope breakdown, and mature stage 14 oocytes are arrested at metaphase I.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila oocyte development.

claim: In Drosophila, mature stage 14 oocytes are arrested at metaphase I.
source: Oocytes in stage 13 undergo nuclear envelope breakdown, and mature stage 14 oocytes are arrested at metaphase I.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila oocyte development.

claim: In Drosophila, egg activation is triggered by rehydration and mechanical stimulation during ovulation.
source: Egg activation is triggered by rehydration and mechanical stimulation during ovulation, just prior to and independently of fertilization (Horner and Wolfner, 2008b; Krauchunas et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Horner and Wolfner, 2008b and Krauchunas et al., 2013.

claim: In Drosophila, Ca2+ signaling is involved in egg activation.
source: In many species, Ca2+ signaling is involved in egg activation (Stricker, 1999); this is true also in Drosophila despite the lack of a role for sperm entry (Kaneuchi et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Stricker, 1999 and Kaneuchi et al., 2015.

claim: When Drosophila activated oocytes are laid without fertilization, they are arrested after the completion of meiosis.
source: When activated oocytes are laid without fertilization (unfertilized activated eggs), they are arrested after the completion of meiosis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila development.

claim: In unfertilized activated Drosophila eggs, maternal mRNAs are translated but mitosis does not begin.
source: Although maternal mRNAs are translated, mitosis does not begin (Doane, 1960; Mahowald et al., 1983; Kronja et al., 2014b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Doane, 1960; Mahowald et al., 1983; Kronja et al., 2014b.

claim: Hundreds of maternal mRNAs are translationally up- or down-regulated during the oocyte-to-embryo transition.
source: Our recent genome-wide study has shown that hundreds of maternal mRNAs are translationally up- or down-regulated during the oocyte-to-embryo transition and that the majority of these translational changes require PNG kinase (Kronja et al., 2014b; Eichhorn et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kronja et al., 2014b and Eichhorn et al., 2016.

claim: The majority of translational changes during the oocyte-to-embryo transition require PNG kinase.
source: Our recent genome-wide study has shown that hundreds of maternal mRNAs are translationally up- or down-regulated during the oocyte-to-embryo transition and that the majority of these translational changes require PNG kinase (Kronja et al., 2014b; Eichhorn et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kronja et al., 2014b and Eichhorn et al., 2016.

claim: png is necessary for initiation of mitosis in the embryo.
source: png was identified originally as a gene necessary for initiation of mitosis in the embryo (Shamanski and Orr-Weaver, 1991).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shamanski and Orr-Weaver, 1991.

claim: png upregulates cyclin B translation during the oocyte-to-embryo transition.
source: This requirement was shown to reflect png upregulating cyclin B (cycB) translation during the oocyte-to-embryo transition (Vardy and Orr-Weaver, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vardy and Orr-Weaver, 2007.

claim: png promotes translation of smg mRNA.
source: Additionally, png was found to promote translation of smg mRNA, thus controlling degradation of maternal mRNAs later in embryogenesis (Tadros et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tadros et al., 2007.

claim: png encodes a Ser/Thr kinase that has two regulatory subunits, PLU and GNU.
source: png encodes a Ser/Thr kinase that has two regulatory subunits, PLU and GNU (Freeman et al., 1986; Fenger et al., 2000; Lee et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Freeman et al., 1986; Fenger et al., 2000; Lee et al., 2003.

claim: PNG forms a complex with PLU and GNU.
source: Our biochemical analysis using purified recombinant proteins demonstrated that PNG forms a complex with PLU and GNU and that GNU dimerizes the PNG-PLU subcomplex to elevate its kinase activity (Lee et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lee et al., 2003.

claim: GNU dimerizes the PNG-PLU subcomplex to elevate its kinase activity.
source: Our biochemical analysis using purified recombinant proteins demonstrated that PNG forms a complex with PLU and GNU and that GNU dimerizes the PNG-PLU subcomplex to elevate its kinase activity (Lee et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lee et al., 2003.

claim: PNG is a known in vitro substrate of PNG kinase.
source: GNU is a known in vitro PNG substrate (Lee et al., 2003), and it is phosphorylated by PNG in these experiments.
evidence: Supported by citation to Lee et al., 2003 and observation in Figure 2C.

claim: PNG activity is not required for the hyperphosphorylated form of GNU in mature oocytes.
source: Mature oocytes from png mutant mothers (png1058/ png1058), however, still have the hyperphosphorylated form of GNU, suggesting that PNG activity is not required for the mobility shift (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: MAPK is active during oocyte maturation.
source: We noted that MAPK, which is active during oocyte maturation (Ivanovska et al., 2004; Sackton et al., 2007) and phosphorylates S/T-P, seems to be dispensable for the slowest mobility GNU phosphorylated form.
evidence: Supported by citations to Ivanovska et al., 2004 and Sackton et al., 2007.

claim: MAPK seems to be dispensable for the slowest mobility GNU phosphorylated form.
source: We noted that MAPK, which is active during oocyte maturation (Ivanovska et al., 2004; Sackton et al., 2007) and phosphorylates S/T-P, seems to be dispensable for the slowest mobility GNU phosphorylated form. In null mutants of mos, the female-meiosis specific MAPK kinase kinase, phosphorylated active MAPK is decreased to less than 10% of wild-type levels, but the mobility of GNU was identical to heterozygous mos sibling controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3 comparing GNU mobility in mos mutants and controls.

claim: In mos null mutants, phosphorylated active MAPK is decreased to less than 10% of wild-type levels.
source: In null mutants of mos, the female-meiosis specific MAPK kinase kinase, phosphorylated active MAPK is decreased to less than 10% of wild-type levels, but the mobility of GNU was identical to heterozygous mos sibling controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.
